teacher_note: People often confuse “bother” (the psychological feeling of being annoyed or disturbed) with “disturb” (interrupting an existing activity).
actionable_tip: Distinction: bother = to cause annoyance; disturb = to interrupt. Example: Don't disturb the class.
example_good: Sorry to bother you so late.

teacher_note: The infinitive often follows “bother”: “bother to do” means “to go to the trouble of doing.”
actionable_tip: Try making sentences:He didn’t bother to reply.
example_good: You don't need to bother to come.
example_bad: You don't need to bother come.

teacher_note: “bother doing” is also common, meaning “to not deign to do something” or “not to bother doing something.”
actionable_tip: Comparison: bother to do vs bother doing: polite/formal vs colloquial usage.
example_bad: I won't bother to calling him.

teacher_note: -er typically denotes “a person/thing,” but not all verbs can form professions or agents by adding -er.
actionable_tip: When encountering a new word, first check the dictionary to see if the derived form actually exists; do not arbitrarily invent words like *botherer.
example_bad: a botherer (rarely used, generally not recommended)

teacher_note: -tion typically turns verbs into nouns: act → action, but not all verbs can be transformed this way.
actionable_tip: Memory: Common nouns ending in -tion are often abstract and have varied usage.
example_bad: do an action (Unnatural in most contexts)

teacher_note: "Action" means to do something or an activity. "Transaction" means a business deal or exchange.
actionable_tip: Use "transaction" for business and money. Use "action" for movies or doing something.

teacher_note: "Ability" is the power to do something (potential). "Skill" is something you learn by practice.
actionable_tip: Use: have the ability to do / develop a skill.
example_good: She has the ability to solve problems.
example_bad: She has the skill to be tall. (Not correct meaning)

teacher_note: Common phrases: ability to do; show/lose/improve ability.
actionable_tip: Example: She showed great ability in math.

teacher_note: Abstract nouns usually do not use an article, like information, advice.
actionable_tip: Avoid: an information (wrong), use: some information / a piece of information.

teacher_note: At first, do not write very long sentences. Make sure subject, verb, and object are clear.
actionable_tip: Each sentence ≤ 12 words. Focus on easy to understand sentences.
example_bad: Because he had some important things to do so he didn’t bother to reply to me which made me sad.

teacher_note: Give two example sentences for one word. Contrast helps you remember.
actionable_tip: Write one positive and one negative, or one abstract and one concrete meaning.
example_good: It doesn’t bother me. / I won’t bother calling.

actionable_tip: Review new words after 24 hours. Review weak words again after 12 hours.
